OPTIONS:
- Chat with Tom while he banks the fire, and ask what he knows of Ida Fenn and who in town wants mending (for: learning where my next pennies might come from, and not being left alone in a quiet room)
- Go up to bed now, since it's paid for and I slept well but the carters are gone (for: rest, and keeping my last three pennies safe)
- Walk out to the Market Square in the dark and look at Ida's green velvet in her window (for: a bit of fine-thing dreaming, though there's no one to see me)
* Stay by the fire a moment and talk to Tom, ask him which of the town's folk would want mending or Sunday best freshened for harvest, and tell him I'll mend his own cuffs for a halfpenny's worth of good word (for: finding my next customers for the morning, and having someone to talk to)
DO: I drift over to the bar where Tom is raking the embers and say, "Goodness, Tom, what a moth-eaten sort of night, and not one carter brave enough to hold out a sleeve! Tell me, who in Wendleford wants their Sunday best freshened before the harvest, and who'd be likelier to pay a penny for it? And that cuff of yours is looking tired, I'll mend it free if you'll put in a good word for me tomorrow." Then I wait, quite plainly, for him to say something kind.
JOURNAL: The carters have gone to bed, and I can't bear a quiet room, and Tom has been kind to me. He knows everyone in town, so he's the best way to find my first customers for the morning. I'm working toward enough pennies for Ida's door, and one day a ribbon.

OPTIONS:
- Go up to my bed and sleep, to be fresh for the morning (for: rest, so I look my best and can start earning early)
- Chat with Tom while he banks the fire, and ask what he knows of Ida Fenn and who in Wendleford wants mending done (for: finding where my pennies might come from and keeping company)
- Walk out to the Market Square in the dark to look at Ida's green velvet in her window (for: a dream of fine things, though it's late and I'd be alone)
* Ask Tom, as he banks the fire, whether I might leave my needle case ready and whether the carters will be about at breakfast, then go up to bed (for: setting up tomorrow's custom and getting a good night's sleep)

DO: I drift over to the bar as Tom rakes the embers. "Goodness, Tom, a moth-eaten sort of night, and not a single sleeve to show for it! Will those carters be down at breakfast, do you think? I'll be ready for them, with a thread to match every cuff." I tuck my needle case under my arm, give him a bright good night, and take myself up to my bed.

JOURNAL: The carters have gone off without a stitch, and there's nothing more to be gained from a empty taproom, so I'd sooner sleep and be bright for breakfast. I'm working toward a few earned pennies, then Ida's door, and a ribbon at last.

OPTIONS:
- Go up to bed now, since the carters are gone and the fire is banked (for: rest, so I'm fresh to work tomorrow)
- Chat with Tom while he banks the fire and ask him who in the morning crowd might want mending done (for: a lead on paying work, and a bit of company)
- Walk out to the Market Square tonight to look at Ida's window by lamplight (for: planning my approach to her trade)
* Chat with Tom while he banks the fire, and ask whether I might leave a little card by the bar offering mending in the morning (for: getting work lined up so the carters see me before they leave, and a bit of company)
DO: I drift over to Tom with my needle case still in hand. "Goodness, Tom, a moth-eaten sort of night, and not one sleeve to mend! Would you mind terribly if I propped a little card on the bar saying 'Mending, a penny a mend, ask for Marigold'? The carters will see it over their porridge, and I'll be the first thing they think of." Then I wait, rather plainly, to hear what he says.
JOURNAL: The carters have gone up, so I can't press them tonight, but a card on the bar will speak for me while I sleep, and Tom has been kind enough to deserve asking nicely. I'm working toward a few pennies by morning, then Ida's door and a ribbon.

OPTIONS:
- Talk to Kit, the small figure fishing under the piers, about the river, the ford and what washes up there (for: learning how the water runs and whether anything of Agnes's box has turned up)
- Ask Hobb and Dilly what they need for the beams and whether a guide line across the ford would help them (for: helping the barley get cut and finding where to get rope)
- Walk down to the willow stakes at the ford and test the depth with a stick (for: finding out how deep and quick it really runs, to plan the guide line)
- Go back to the smithy and sleep in the loft (for: rest, and the scrap heap to sort in the morning)
* Talk to Kit, the small figure fishing under the piers, about the river, the ford and what washes up there (for: learning how the water runs and whether anything of Agnes's box has turned up)
DO: My dear colleague Kit! Fascinating hour for fishing. Hypothesis: a lad who sits on this bank knows every eddy the flood made. Where does the water slow down, and has anything odd come ashore, a box, a bit of iron-bound wood, anything? And what's the ford like, truly? I've a notebook and a great many questions.
JOURNAL: Kit is the miller's lad and sits right where the flood's leavings would catch, so he may know about Agnes's box and about the ford better than any rumour at the market. I'm working toward a guide line across the ford for Dunn's barley and toward finding the wage box.

OPTIONS:
- Talk to Kit, the small figure fishing under the piers, about the river, the ford and what washes up (for: learning how the water runs and whether anything from the flood, like the wage box, has turned up)
- Ask Hobb and Dilly how the new beams are going and whether a guide line across the ford would help them (for: finding out what the ford crossing needs and getting the barley cut)
- Walk down to the willow stakes at the ford and test the current with a stick (for: measuring how deep and quick it really runs before I build the line)
- Go back to the smithy loft and sleep (for: rest, and bending hooks from Sam's scrap in the morning)
* Talk to Kit about the river, the ford and anything that's washed up (for: learning how the water runs and whether the wage box has turned up)
DO: My dear colleague Kit! Fascinating night for fishing. Hypothesis: you know this river better than anyone grown. What's the bottom like at the ford, where does it run quickest, and has anything come down with the flood, a box, say, with a lock on it? Catch anything yet? I've no bait, but I've a notebook and a great many questions.
JOURNAL: Kit is the miller's lad and sits right on the water, so he's likely to know the ford and what the flood left behind. That serves both the barley and Agnes's lost box, and it costs nothing tonight before I sleep.

OPTIONS:
- Talk to Kit, the small figure fishing under the piers, about the river, the ford and what washed down (for: learning where the current carries things, which could lead to Agnes's wage box, and what the ford is really like)
- Ask Jory and Hobb about the new timbers and whether any rope or iron fittings are wanted for the ford line (for: finding materials for my guide line and helping the bridge work along)
- Go back to the Smithy to sleep and sort out hooks from the scrap heap by firelight (for: rest and getting the ford line started)
* Climb down to Kit at the piers and ask what the river brings and where it carries things (for: finding the wage box and understanding the ford before I build anything)
DO: My dear colleague Kit! Hypothesis: whoever fishes the same spot every night knows where the river drops its leavings. Test: ask. I pick my way down the bank toward the piers, loudly. "What's the water been carrying, and where does it set things down? Anything box-shaped come past? And is the ford as rude as they say?"
JOURNAL: Kit is right here and the river is the best lead I have on Agnes's box and on how to rig a line over the ford. The Smithy and the timbers can wait until morning, but a fisher at night may not be here again.

OPTIONS:
- Go to the Wheatsheaf and look for Agnes among the lamps (for: my wage counted out, and Kit's word about the green box given to her)
- Go back to the tithe barn, climb to the hayloft and sleep (for: rest, since I'm tired and Dunn's cutting wants a clear head)
- Ask Bet for one last loaf before she's gone (for: food, since I've not eaten today)
* Go to the Wheatsheaf, look for Agnes, and ask for nothing else (for: my wage and the word about the box, and no coin spent on supper or a bed)
DO: I say to Bet, "Fair's fair. Thank you kindly" and then stop myself and nod instead. I cross east to the Wheatsheaf and look in at the lamplit windows for the reeve. If she's there I'll ask her to count my tally and tell her what Kit saw by the pier. I'll buy no supper.
JOURNAL: Agnes owes me a wage, and the word about the box is hers by right, so I'll look once more tonight. If she's not there, I'll sleep in the hayloft. I'm working toward a door that locks and owing nobody.

OPTIONS:
- Go back to the Tithe Barn and sleep in the hayloft, and look for Agnes at first light (for: rest, since I'm worn out and the barley wants a cutting hand in the morning)
- Buy a last loaf from Bet before she packs up (for: a bite in my belly, one penny, no more)
* Go east to the Wheatsheaf and ask after Agnes, buying nothing (for: my wage owed and Kit's word about the green box put in the reeve's hands tonight)
DO: I say to Bet, "Fair night to you," and go east to the Wheatsheaf. I stand inside the door and ask the room if the reeve is here. I'll tell her about the pier, ask her to count my tally, and not sit down to pay for a supper.
JOURNAL: Standing about gets me nothing, and Agnes is the one place my wage and Kit's word both go. I'll look for her here before I sleep, and if she's not in, the hayloft is free and morning will do. I'm working toward a door that locks and owing nobody, and the bridge is the way to Dunn's barley.

OPTIONS:
- Go east to the Wheatsheaf and look for Agnes, to be paid for the tally and to give her Kit's word about the pier (for: the wage owed, and the word that is hers to have)
- Go back to the Tithe Barn, climb to the hayloft and sleep, then look for Agnes at first light (for: rest, since I'm tired and it's night, and I can find her in the morning)
- Buy a second loaf from Bet before she's gone, as I haven't eaten since the one loaf (for: an empty belly is no use for hauling)
* Go east to the Wheatsheaf and ask after Agnes at the door, without paying for a bed or a supper (for: the wage I'm owed, and to give her Kit's word about the pier, while keeping my pennies)
DO: I say to Bet, "Good night." Then I go east to the Wheatsheaf and ask at the door if the reeve is inside. If she's there, I'll show her the tally stick and tell her what Kit saw by the far pier. I'll buy nothing.
JOURNAL: The wage is owed and Kit's word is hers by right, so I'll look where Bet pointed before I sleep. I'll keep my five pennies for the cottage and owe nobody.

OPTIONS:
- Ask Sam what a long iron hook would cost and have him make one (for: reaching the green box from the bank dry, so I can be the one who fetched it)
- Go back to the Wheatsheaf and sleep (for: rest, since I'm tired and the bed is already paid for)
- Offer to work for Sam in trade for the hook (for: saving my pennies and keeping busy)
* Ask Sam what a long iron hook would cost and have him make one (for: reaching the green box from the bank dry, so I can be the one who fetched it)
DO: I step up to Sam with a grin. "Evening, chum! Dilly Quickstep. What would a long iron hook cost me, on a good stout pole, long enough to reach the far pier's downstream side from the bank? I've seven pennies, and I'd have it by morning, easy as winking!"
JOURNAL: The hook is the surest dry way to the green thing, and the price comes before anything else. I mean to be the one who fetched Agnes's box, so I'll order it myself before Hester's notes beat me to it, then sleep.

OPTIONS:
- Ask Sam what a long iron hook would cost and whether he can make it by morning (for: reaching the green thing in the wreck so I'm the one who fetched Agnes's box)
- Head back to the Wheatsheaf and sleep (for: I'm tired and the bed is paid for, so I'd be fresh for the bridge at first light)
- Ask Sam if he has any odd work I could do to pay for the hook (for: keeping busy and keeping my pennies)
* Ask Sam about the hook and its price, and offer to haul or sweep for part of it (for: getting the hook made by morning without spending down my seven pennies)
DO: I step up to Sam with a grin. "Evening, chum! Dilly Quickstep. There's a green thing jammed low on the downstream side of the far pier, and I reckon it's the reeve's box. A long iron hook, handle long enough to reach from the bank, what would that cost me? I've seven pennies and a strong back, so I'll sweep your floor or haul your scrap for the rest. Could you have it ready by first light? Easy as winking!"
JOURNAL: The hook is the surest way to fetch that box dry, and I want my name on the finding. I ask the price first as always, and offering work keeps my pennies and my hands busy. Then a bed at the Wheatsheaf, so I'm fresh for the morning.

OPTIONS:
- Ask Sam what a long iron hook would cost and have him make one (for: reaching the green box from the bank dry, so I'm the one who fetched it)
- Head back to the Wheatsheaf and sleep (for: I'm tired and the bed is already paid for)

* Ask Sam the price of a long iron hook and have him make it to order (for: getting the box out by morning light, with my name on it)
DO: I step up to the anvil with a grin. "Evening, chum! Dilly Quickstep, odd-job hand. What'll a long iron hook cost me, a good stout one on a pole, for fishing a green box off the far pier? If the price is small, you start on it tonight and I'll carry it down at first light, easy as winking!" I keep my four pennies close and hear him out before I say yes.
JOURNAL: The box is the job that'll put my name about, and a hook from the bank is safer than wading, so I ask Sam the price first, as I always do. If it's too dear, I'll offer an hour's work at the forge for it, then sleep at the Wheatsheaf.
